Like most stick insects, leaf insects are capable of parthenogenetic reproduction.
Depending on the species, each female lays between 100 and 300 eggs in this manner.
The eggs - laid at a rate of one to three per week - are either dropped to the ground or flung away via a sudden, jerky movement of the abdomen.
The freshly hatched nymphs, which are initially very strikingly colored, hatch after four to eight months by pushing open the lid with their heads.
Development into an adult insect takes four to eight months, depending on the species and sex; males molt four times and females six times.
They do this so accurately that predators often are not able to distinguish them from real leaves.
To further confuse predators, when the leaf insect walks, it rocks back and forth, mimicking a real leaf being blown by the wind.
Females produce an egg sac before they molt.
In the wild, females take around 9–10 years to reach maturity, but can then live for another 10 years.
Males can take 7–8 years to reach maturity, afterwards usually dying within a year.
In a large well planted aquarium, a single pair of emperor tetras will often breed without any extra stimulation.
